key_cases.case_name: Idaho Department of Health & Welfare v. Doe (2016-11)
key_cases.holding: Affirming termination, the court held that the Department satisfied I.C. § 16-1621(3)(c) by developing four case plans identifying the issues, the parent's tasks and the Department's own role, and that substantial and competent evidence supported the findings of neglect, inability to discharge parental responsibilities, and best interests.
key_cases.relevance: The leading Idaho application of the CPA reasonable-reunification-efforts requirement in I.C. § 16-1621(3)(c).
key_cases.quote: We hold that the magistrate court did not err by finding that the IDHW made reasonable efforts to reunify Mother with her children

key_cases.case_name: Idaho Department of Health & Welfare v. Doe
key_cases.holding: Affirming termination, the court held that the Department's reunification efforts and its placement choices are CPA requirements that are not relevant to whether the statutory grounds for termination are proved, and that the mother's due-process rights were protected by the clear-and-convincing burden at the termination trial.
key_cases.relevance: Holds that dissatisfaction with reunification efforts does not defeat a termination supported by clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.quote: those cases also demonstrate that such findings are irrelevant to termination proceedings because reasonable efforts are requirements under the CPA, not Idaho's parental-rights termination statute

key_cases.holding: The court vacated a termination order and remanded, holding that the rebuttable presumption in I.C. § 16-1629(9) favors only the Department's filing of a termination petition after fifteen of twenty-two months in care and does not shift to the parent the burden of disproving that termination is in the child's best interests.
key_cases.relevance: Preserves Idaho's longstanding presumption that a natural parent should have custody of his children.
key_cases.quote: It does not create a presumption that it is in the best interests of the child to terminate parental rights

key_cases.case_name: Roe v. State, Department of Health & Welfare
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed denial of a grandmother's motion to intervene, holding that the CPA confers no conditional right to intervene, that permissive intervention under I.R.C.P. 24(b)(2) is inconsistent with the CPA, and that once the Department has legal custody it, not the court, decides where the child lives.
key_cases.relevance: Confirms the court's retained but limited authority to approve or refuse return of the child to the home from which removal occurred.
key_cases.quote: Once the Department has legal custody of a child under the CPA, the Department and not the court has the authority to determine where the child should live

key_cases.holding: The court reversed a magistrate's decree terminating an unmarried biological father's parental rights and remanded, holding that although the magistrate's factual findings were supported by substantial and competent evidence he failed to apply the correct law, because a father who had filed a notarized acknowledgment of paternity with the mother's consent was entitled to notice of the termination hearing under I.C. §§ 16-2007 and 16-1505(1)(d).
key_cases.relevance: Reverses the termination and directs that custody and visitation be arranged for the biological father, applying Idaho's presumption that a natural parent should have custody as against non-parents.
key_cases.quote: The magistrate judge's factual findings are supported by substantial and competent evidence, but he failed to apply the correct law to the facts of this case.

key_cases.case_name: Idaho Department of Health & Welfare v. Doe
key_cases.holding: Affirming termination as to both parents, the court held that I.C. § 16-1624 authorizes the Department to petition for termination once the court has found CPA jurisdiction at the adjudicatory hearing and placed the child in the Department's legal custody or protective supervision, so neither due process nor the termination statute's purpose provision requires that the parent first be given a full opportunity to complete a case plan.
key_cases.relevance: Holds that the CPA's reunification framework does not condition the Department's termination petition, so dissatisfaction with reunification efforts is not by itself a defense to termination.
key_cases.quote: Thus, under the authority granted by the CPA, the Department is authorized to petition for termination if the court has jurisdiction over the child under the CPA
